title: Baltimore students sue over AI that allegedly mistook Doritos bag for gun

 Thao Nguyen USA TODAY Updated Nov. 19, 2026, 1:38 a.m. ET Hear this story Four current and former students of a Baltimore high school have filed a lawsuit against a school district, police department and artificial intelligence company, alleging they were handcuffed and searched after a weapon detection system falsely alerted authorities to a gun that turned out to be a bag of chips.
 The lawsuit, filed Nov. 17 in Baltimore County Circuit Court, names Omnilert, Baltimore County Public Schools, school officials, the Baltimore County Police Department and individual officers as defendants. The plaintiffs allege their constitutional rights were violated during an Oct. 20, 2025, incident outside Kenwood High School.
 According to the complaint, the students were waiting for a ride home after football practice when officers responded to an alert generated by Omnilert's AI weapon detection system. The lawsuit alleges the students were suddenly surrounded by Baltimore County Police Department officers, many with guns drawn.
 Officers then "forced the students to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched them" before determining there was no weapon, according to the lawsuit. The teens, who are Black, allege the system incorrectly identified a bag of Cool Ranch Doritos one of the students was holding as a firearm.
 Attorneys representing the students said the AI system issued an alert indicating there was a 90% probability a gun was present on campus. According to the complaint, school and police personnel quickly determined the alert was invalid and canceled it. But despite the cancellation, an armed police response was still dispatched because of failures in communication and notification procedures, attorneys said.
 "The police told my son this could have been a real problem. No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother," Freida Winfield, who was on her way to pick up her son and the other students when the incident occurred, said in a statement .

 The lawsuit was filed by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, along with Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP and Engel Law Group, P.C.. The nonprofit legal organization said the case raises broader questions about the use of artificial intelligence in public safety and schools and whether sufficient safeguards exist to prevent false alerts from escalating into law enforcement responses.
 The group said it is seeking reforms to require schools and police to verify reports from AI threat-detection systems and adopt policies to prevent false alerts from triggering armed police responses. It also called for greater training, oversight and transparency surrounding the technology's use.
 "These students were failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts, but also by the very adults meant to keep them safe when we send them to school," Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said in a statement announcing the lawsuit .
 The Baltimore County Police Department said it was unable to comment on pending litigation. USA TODAY reached out to Baltimore County Public Schools and Omnilert for comment.

 The incident was previously investigated by the Maryland Office of the Inspector General for Education , which issued a report in November 2025 after reviewing district policies, procedures, training, and notification protocols.
 The report found that school staff and a police representative reviewed the alert shortly after it was generated and determined it was not a credible threat. A cancellation notice was then sent to personnel receiving the alert.
 The agency concluded the incident escalated because a school employee failed to notice the cancellation and shared a screenshot with a law enforcement officer, ultimately resulting in a police response. The agency said it could not substantiate allegations that the Omnilert system was ineffective, inefficient, or biased and concluded that "human error and training gaps" led to the incident.
 The report also found the system did not specifically identify a potato chip bag as a gun. Rather, the agency said the alert was triggered by the student's position, hand movements, and the reflective properties of an object visible in the image.
